title: A T. Rex Would Ignore You. This Dinosaur Would Chase You.
description: A skull fragment sat in a London museum drawer for nearly 100 years. In October 2026 scientists named it Invictibellatrix amberina, a tiger-sized, long-clawed T. rex cousin from the Isle of Wight. Its lead researcher says that for humans it would have been more dangerous than a T. rex.

facts.claim: Invictibellatrix amberina, a new megaraptoran dinosaur identified from a fossil found on the Isle of Wight, lived around 120 million years ago; published in Royal Society Open Science

Lead researcher: for humans it would have been more dangerous than a T. rex; we would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight; they definitely would have chased us; a T. rex would not have bothered as we would have been too small
About the size of a large tiger; 3-4 m (10 to 13 feet) long and just over 1.5 m tall, about as tall as a human (almost 5 feet / about 5 feet); likely had feathers
Megaraptorans had relatively narrow skulls, powerful arms and huge curved claws to seize prey rather than relying mainly on massive jaws; its claws might have been about 10-20 cm (4-8 inches)
It would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals, a role in the food chain similar to the hyena today
The fossil is part of the rear of the skull; the Natural History Museum in London acquired it in 1924, and it sat in a drawer for nearly 100 years
CT scans and anatomical comparisons indicated a previously unidentified dinosaur
The name translates to 'unconquered female warrior'
Some later megaraptorans developed claws up to 35 cm (14 inches) long

careful: What-if framing: the chase is clearly hypothetical, and the script says humans never met it. Size and claw lengths are given as estimates ('scientists estimate', 'maybe'). The researcher and the fossil collector are not named or shown. No blood or injury is shown. The 'you' hiker and the lab worker are faceless mannequins. Image prompts describe the fossil as a 'bone fragment' and the animal's 'front limbs'.

trend.why_now: Invictibellatrix amberina was announced October 14, 2026 under 'would have chased us / more dangerous than a T. rex' headlines (CBS, ScienceDaily), and outlets are still covering it: EarthSky published October 19 and updated October 25, and Earth.com ran it November 1. Our best-performing Short ever is the T. rex survival what-if (11.4x), so this is a direct follow-up for the same audience.
trend.pattern: This follows the news hook 'more dangerous to humans than a T. rex / would have chased us' and the setup of our own T. rex what-if hit. The viewer is prey in the first second, then gets sized against the animal, then comes the twist that the fossil sat in a drawer for a century. The title is a contrast pair: 'X would ignore you. This would chase you.'
